lead: This unit builds lattices from partial orders and then adds the laws that make a Boolean algebra. You learn to check closure, draw Hasse diagrams, use complements and write Boolean functions in DNF and CNF. After it you can test whether a poset is a lattice and whether a subset or a map preserves the operations.
about: The unit starts with 5.1, which reads a lattice both as a poset with joins and meets and as an algebraic system with two operations. 5.2 proves the basic identities and defines a sublattice by closure. 5.3 adds direct products and lattice homomorphisms, a topic only a few universities teach. 5.4 separates bounded, complemented and distributive lattices, and shows why complements are unique only under distributivity. 5.5 turns the bounded distributive complemented lattice into a Boolean algebra and lists its laws. 5.6 writes Boolean functions as Boolean polynomials, with canonical DNF and CNF. 5.7 closes with sub-Boolean algebras and Boolean homomorphisms. Each chapter uses Hasse diagrams and small finite examples, so the definitions stay visible. The advanced chapters are shorter because only a few universities teach them as separate topics.

chapters.idea: A lattice is a partially ordered set (poset) in which every pair of elements has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound, and the same structure can be described by two algebraic operations.
chapters.depth: Recap partial order and Hasse diagram from Unit 2. Define upper bound, lower bound, least upper bound (join, supremum, ∨) and greatest lower bound (meet, infimum, ∧) for a pair. A poset is a lattice when every pair has both. Show finite examples: a chain, the divisors of 12 under divisibility, the diamond, and a poset that fails because two upper bounds have no least one. Then define an algebraic lattice (L,∨,∧) by idempotent, commutative, associative and absorption laws. State that the two definitions are equivalent; prove the absorption-to-order step. Mention duality: swap ∨ with ∧ and reverse ≤. Some syllabi call the poset version a lattice as a poset and the operation version a lattice as an algebraic system.

figure.aria: Hasse diagram of the divisors of 12 ordered by divisibility, with 1 at the bottom and 12 at the top.

chapters.example: Let A={1,2,3,4,6,12} be ordered by divisibility: a≤b means a divides b. Show A is a lattice. For the pair 4 and 6, the upper bounds in A are 12, so 4∨6=12; the lower bounds are 1 and 2, so 4∧6=2. For 2 and 3, the upper bounds are 6 and 12, so 2∨3=6; the lower bound is 1, so 2∧3=1. Every pair has a join and a meet, so A is a lattice.
chapters.trap: Treating any upper bound as the least upper bound. A poset can have upper bounds for a pair and still fail to be a lattice when no least one exists.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: partial orders and Hasse diagrams.
chapters.leave: Properties of lattices, sublattices, special lattices and Boolean algebra go to 5.2, 5.4 and 5.5.

chapters.idea: In every lattice the join and meet operations obey a fixed set of identities, and a sublattice is a nonempty subset closed under both operations.
chapters.depth: Derive idempotent, commutative, associative and absorption laws from the poset definition; show a∨(a∧b)=a and its dual. Add monotonicity: a≤b implies a∨c≤b∨c and a∧c≤b∧c. Define a sublattice as a nonempty subset S of L closed under ∨ and ∧, with the inherited order. Test S={1,2,4,12} inside the divisors of 12; test T={1,2,3,12} and show 2∨3=6 leaves T. Distinguish a sublattice from a subposet: a subposet may not be closed. Mention that a bounded sublattice must contain the same 0 and 1 if it is to keep the bounds. Some syllabi write sub-lattice.

figure.aria: Hasse diagram of the divisors of 12 with the subset S equal to 1, 2, 4 and 12 highlighted.

chapters.example: In A={1,2,3,4,6,12} under divisibility, test S={1,2,4,12}. Compute 2∨4=4, 2∧4=2, 4∨12=12, 4∧12=4, 2∨12=12, 2∧12=2, and 1∨x=x, 1∧x=1 for every x. All results lie in S, so S is a sublattice. Test T={1,2,3,12}. Here 2∨3=6 and 6∉T, so T is not a sublattice. T is still a subposet of A.
chapters.trap: Checking closure under only one operation. A sublattice needs both join and meet computed in the parent lattice, and it must be nonempty.
chapters.leave: Products and homomorphisms go to 5.3; distributivity and complements go to 5.4.

chapters.idea: A direct product combines lattices coordinate by coordinate, and a lattice homomorphism is a map that preserves join and meet.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic. Define the direct product L1×L2 with order (a,b)≤(c,d) iff a≤c and b≤d, and operations coordinatewise. The product of two lattices is a lattice. Define lattice homomorphism h:L→M by h(a∨b)=h(a)∨h(b) and h(a∧b)=h(a)∧h(b); isomorphism if h is bijective. Show the projection π1(a,b)=a is a homomorphism. Show f(a,b)=a∨b is order-preserving but not a meet-homomorphism. Mention that kernel is not used as in groups; congruences are a later topic. Some syllabi call the product a product lattice.

figure.aria: Hasse diagram of the product lattice L × L for L = {0,1}, with bottom 00 and top 11.

chapters.example: Let L={0,1} with 0<1. The product L×L has elements 00,01,10,11, ordered by (a,b)≤(c,d) iff a≤c and b≤d. Its join is coordinatewise OR and its meet is coordinatewise AND. Check the projection π1(a,b)=a. For 10 and 01, π1(10∨01)=π1(11)=1 and π1(10)∨π1(01)=1∨0=1. Also π1(10∧01)=π1(00)=0 and π1(10)∧π1(01)=1∧0=0. So π1 preserves both operations and is a lattice homomorphism. The map f(a,b)=a∨b sends 10 and 01 to 1, but f(10∧01)=f(00)=0 while f(10)∧f(01)=1, so f is not a meet-homomorphism.
chapters.trap: Assuming every order-preserving map is a lattice homomorphism. The map f(a,b)=a∨b preserves order but can fail meet preservation.
chapters.leave: Special lattices go to 5.4; Boolean homomorphisms go to 5.7.

chapters.idea: Bounded, complemented and distributive lattices are separated by extra laws, and together they describe a Boolean lattice.
chapters.depth: Define a bounded lattice with bottom 0 and top 1; identities a∨0=a and a∧1=a. Define a complement: b is a complement of a when a∨b=1 and a∧b=0; a complemented lattice has a complement for every element, not necessarily unique. Define a distributive lattice by a∧(b∨c)=(a∧b)∨(a∧c), and note the dual identity is equivalent. Examples: every chain is distributive; the divisor lattice of 12 is distributive; the diamond M3 and pentagon N5 are not. In a distributive lattice a complement is unique. A Boolean lattice is a bounded distributive complemented lattice. Some syllabi call 0 and 1 the least and greatest elements.

figure.aria: Hasse diagram of the diamond M3 with bottom 0, top 1, and three middle elements a, b and c.

chapters.example: In the diamond M3={0,a,b,c,1}, let 0 be the bottom, 1 the top, and a,b,c be the three middle elements with no order among them. Compute a∧(b∨c)=a∧1=a. Compute (a∧b)∨(a∧c)=0∨0=0. Since a≠0, M3 is not distributive. Also a∨b=1 and a∧b=0, and a∨c=1 and a∧c=0, so a has two complements b and c. This shows complements need not be unique without distributivity.
chapters.trap: Reading complemented as unique complement. Uniqueness needs distributivity; M3 gives one element two complements.
chapters.leave: Boolean algebra laws go to 5.5; Boolean functions go to 5.6.

chapters.idea: A Boolean algebra is a bounded distributive complemented lattice, equivalently an algebraic system with join, meet, complement, 0 and 1 obeying a compact set of laws.
chapters.depth: Define Boolean algebra in two equivalent ways: a bounded distributive complemented lattice, and an algebraic system (B,∨,∧,′,0,1) with commutative, distributive, identity and complement laws. State 0≠1. Derive idempotent, bounded, absorption, involution and De Morgan laws; list both De Morgan laws. Show B2={0,1} and P(S) under union, intersection and complement are Boolean algebras. Explain duality: swap ∨ with ∧ and 0 with 1. Show complement is unique. Some texts call the axiom set Huntington's postulates. Some syllabi call the operations sum and product or write + and ·; keep ∨ and ∧ for lattices.

figure.title: Conditions for a Boolean algebra
figure.aria: Flow of conditions from a lattice to a bounded distributive complemented lattice, which is a Boolean algebra.

chapters.example: Let U={1,2,3} and B=P(U), with A={1,2} and C={2,3}. Here ∨ is union, ∧ is intersection, and ′ is complement in U. Compute A∨C={1,2,3}=U, A∧C={2}, A′={3}, C′={1}. Check De Morgan: (A∨C)′=U′=∅ and A′∧C′={3}∩{1}=∅. Also A∨A′=U and A∧A′=∅, so A′ is the complement of A.
chapters.trap: Mixing the two distributive laws. In a Boolean algebra a∨(b∧c)=(a∨b)∧(a∨c), not (a∨b)∧c; also 0 and 1 must be distinct.
chapters.leave: Boolean polynomials and normal forms go to 5.6; subalgebras and homomorphisms go to 5.7.

chapters.idea: Every Boolean function can be written as a Boolean polynomial, and the canonical forms are DNF and CNF built from minterms and maxterms.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach Boolean functions as a separate chapter; it extends the normal forms from Unit 1. Define f:{0,1}^n→{0,1}; a Boolean polynomial is an expression in variables using ∨,∧,′. Define literal, minterm (product with every variable once, complemented or not) and maxterm (sum with every variable once). Canonical DNF is the OR of minterms where f=1; canonical CNF is the AND of maxterms where f=0. Show the XOR function f(x,y)=x′y+xy′ has DNF x′y+xy′ and CNF (x+y)(x′+y′). State every Boolean function has such forms. Some syllabi write sum of products for DNF and product of sums for CNF.

figure.title: XOR: f = x′y + xy′
figure.aria: Truth table for XOR on two variables, listing the minterms m1 and m2 where f is 1 and the maxterms M0 and M3 where f is 0.

chapters.example: Let f(x,y)=x′y+xy′ (XOR). Its truth table has f=1 at 01 and 10, and f=0 at 00 and 11. The minterms are m1=x′y and m2=xy′, so the canonical DNF is f=x′y+xy′. The maxterms are M0=x+y and M3=x′+y′, so the canonical CNF is f=(x+y)(x′+y′). Check input 10: DNF gives 0·0+1·1=1; CNF gives (1+0)(0+1)=1. Check input 11: DNF gives 0·1+1·0=0; CNF gives (1+1)(0+0)=0.
chapters.trap: Using maxterms in a DNF or leaving a variable out of a minterm. Canonical DNF uses minterms where f=1; canonical CNF uses maxterms where f=0.
chapters.leave: Sub-Boolean algebras and Boolean homomorphisms go to 5.7.

chapters.idea: A sub-Boolean algebra is a subset closed under join, meet and complement and containing 0 and 1, while a Boolean homomorphism preserves all three operations and the two constants.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic. Define a sub-Boolean algebra S of B: S⊆B, S contains 0 and 1, and S is closed under ∨, ∧ and ′. Show S={∅,{1},{2,3},U} inside P({1,2,3}) is a sub-Boolean algebra; show {∅,{1},{2},{1,2,3}} fails because {1}∪{2}={1,2} is missing. Define Boolean homomorphism h:B→B2 by h(a∨b)=h(a)∨h(b), h(a∧b)=h(a)∧h(b), h(a′)=h(a)′, h(0)=0 and h(1)=1; isomorphism if bijective. Test the map h(A)=1 when 1∈A else 0. Some syllabi call S a Boolean subalgebra.

figure.aria: Hasse diagram of the power set of {1,2,3}; the highlighted nodes ∅, 1, 23 and 123 form a sub-Boolean algebra.

chapters.example: Let U={1,2,3} and B=P(U). Let S={∅,{1},{2,3},U}. Check closure: {1}∪{2,3}=U, {1}∩{2,3}=∅, {1}′={2,3}, {2,3}′={1}, ∅′=U, U′=∅. So S is a sub-Boolean algebra. Define h:B→{0,1} by h(A)=1 if 1∈A, else 0. For A={1,2} and C={2,3}, h(A∨C)=h(U)=1 and h(A)∨h(C)=1∨0=1; h(A∧C)=h({2})=0 and h(A)∧h(C)=1∧0=0; h(A′)=h({3})=0 and h(A)′=1′=0. Also h(∅)=0 and h(U)=1, so h is a Boolean homomorphism.
chapters.trap: Checking only closure under join and meet. A sub-Boolean algebra also needs complement closure and both 0 and 1; a Boolean homomorphism must preserve complement and the constants.
chapters.leave: Applications such as switching circuits are outside this unit.
